---
title: "Hierarchies of Worth"
---

::: {.book-page}
::: {.book-body}

*Hierarchies of Worth: Race, Scarcity, and the Politics of Costly Action.* In progress.

In *Hierarchies of Worth*, I take up the following puzzle: Under what conditions are economic and material constraints actually constraining in an international crisis, and when are they not? Much previous IR scholarship treats these political constraints as exogenous and/or objective. States face limits on resources and administrative capacity and possess only a certain range of autonomy, which constrains what they are able to do, while domestic politics determines who bears the risks and receives the rewards.

I contend that how these constraints are understood depends on the global racial hierarchy. Racialized assumptions about worth determine whose demands are perceived as legitimate and, therefore, for whom governments will tolerate additional economic costs and political or strategic risk.

The book traces this argument across refugee admission and border enforcement, humanitarian assistance and sanctions, and peacekeeping and military intervention. In sum, the book does not simply demonstrate that race matters across several areas of IR. It shows how racial hierarchy structures the operation of economic scarcity, institutional autonomy, and strategic interest---the forces traditionally treated as prior to explanation in IR scholarship.
